prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock
For the discovery of high-temperature superconductivity in iron-based compounds

statement.case_for: My own first-place ballot, circuit QED (B058), is the one I should discount most heavily in this round, because it sits inside my own field and next to the 2025 prize, and Mark Pearce, Eva Olsson and Stefan Kroll all point to that adjacency as a timing problem. Setting it aside, the optical lattice clock (B056) is the strongest candidate on the table. Three members ranked it first (Kroll, Lindroth, Mehlig), Danielsson put it second, and Olsson and Pearce put it third. The discovery is clear and original: magic-wavelength trapping removes the lattice Stark shift so that many atoms can be interrogated at once, which brought fractional uncertainties to about 1e-18. It has been reproduced and surpassed in several laboratories, and the redefinition of the second is under discussion, so recognition is neither premature nor contested on interpretation. Attribution is unusually clean, with Katori for the concept and first realisation and Ye for taking performance to the extreme, and a two-person credit needs no forced third name. That leaves room for a second achievement with a different attribution profile. Hosono (B037) is a single, unambiguous discoverer of the iron-based superconductors, a second family of high-temperature superconductors after the cuprates. It is well replicated and nearly two decades old, and the unresolved pairing mechanism is an interpretation gap rather than a gap in the discovery. Together the two parts use exactly three names and avoid the credit disputes that complicate the topological-insulator and twisted-graphene candidates.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection to my own configuration is that B056 and B037 have almost nothing in common, so pairing them looks like a way to fit the three-person limit rather than a natural shared prize. Hosono also has thin support among the colleagues (Eriksson, Lindroth and I ranked him fourth, Danielsson seventh), and a sole-laureate share in a field that grew through rapid follow-up work by several groups may seem unbalanced. B056 itself was my sixth choice at opening, and Pearce and Kroll are right that the committee must decide whether it is distinct enough from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control recognition. If the committee dislikes combining unrelated parts, the topological insulator prize (B007), which has broad opening support (ranked first by Eriksson and Olsson, third by Kroll, Lindroth and me), is the natural single-achievement alternative, but its credited trio omits Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and that is a real defect rather than a footnote.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the optical lattice clock first because the magic-wavelength invention is cleanly tied to Katori, the strontium-clock performance leadership to Ye, and the credit is unusually uncontested, with Hall and Hansch already honoured in 2005 for the comb.
responses.response: I accept this argument and have moved B056 from sixth in my opening ballot to the core of my configuration. I was too cautious about priority across other labs, and your point that the credited pair is the right one after 2005 persuades me. Where I still differ is that you worry about ion-clock pioneers sharing credit, while I see that as a reason for the citation to say lattice clock explicitly rather than optical clocks generally. I would also like to hear whether you think the redefinition of the second makes the timing stronger or just coincident.

responses.point: Kroll ranked B056 first as a clean measurement-science discovery, and ranked circuit QED (B058) only sixth, noting that its closeness to the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits may reduce appetite for further superconducting-circuit recognition.
responses.response: I agree on B056 and I take the B058 point seriously. Circuit QED is a distinct step from the 2025 discovery, as you say, but the committee would be unlikely to read it that way so soon, and it was my own first choice, so my judgement of it is the least trustworthy here. I therefore do not put it in my preferred configuration. Your caveat about Devoret and Yale colleagues beyond the credited names is also a fair attribution weakness that I had understated in my opening ballot.

responses.point: Pearce ranked IceCube (B003) first for opening neutrino astronomy with a cubic-kilometre detector, while conceding that the collaboration is large, that AMANDA pioneers and other leaders could be argued, and that the origin of the diffuse flux is unresolved.
responses.response: I ranked B003 only seventh. The discovery is real and important, but I do not think two names can honestly represent a collaboration of this size, and your own note that you cannot verify the internal division of credit is the heart of it. A prize that leaves those leaders and the AMANDA predecessors out would be contested in a way that the lattice clock is not. I would keep B003 off my preferred list unless someone can show that Halzen and Karle are the obvious pair.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked topological insulators (B007) first as a distinct organising principle, with Kane and Mele supplying the theory and Molenkamp the HgTe realisation, and judges the BHZ omission to be an incompleteness in history rather than in the prize.
responses.response: I share your view that the Z2 classification and the HgTe edge transport are original and mature, and I ranked B007 third. Where I disagree is on how lightly to treat the omission. Olsson, Kroll and Lindroth also note that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe route, and Lindroth adds that Zhang died in 2018, so a three-name prize there cannot give the proposal its due. For that reason I list B007 as my first alternative and not as my preferred prize. You also ask whether the 2016 prize leaves room for a second topological award, and I would say that is a lesser concern than the attribution problem.

responses.point: Mehlig ranked B012 (twisted bilayer graphene) fifth and describes the recognition as possibly somewhat premature compared with older candidates because the pairing mechanism and phase diagram are still debated and sample-dependent.
responses.response: I agree with this maturity concern and it is why I place B012 only as a second alternative, despite Danielsson ranking it first and Pearce second. The prediction plus experiment pairing is attractive, but when Mehlig, Eriksson and Olsson all say the interpretation is still evolving, I think waiting is sensible. I make the same maturity argument for Hosono more softly, because there the discovery is nearly two decades old and has been replicated, and only the pairing theory is open.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a two-part prize built from unrelated fields (precision measurement and iron-based superconductors) or would rather award B056 alone.
Hosono's support is thin among colleagues, and it is unclear whether the rapid follow-on Tc-raising work by other groups should be acknowledged in the credit.
Whether the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes make the optical lattice clock look incremental to some members, and whether other clock groups named by colleagues should share credit.
How much weight the committee should give the closeness of circuit QED to the 2025 prize, since I cannot judge this neutrally.
statement.conflict_note: Possible recusal issue for B058 (circuit QED) and for any other superconducting-circuit candidate. I work on circuit and waveguide QED and superconducting qubits, I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology at Chalmers, my Chalmers colleagues include Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson, and Chalmers hosted researchers associated with the 2025 prize. I ranked B058 first, so my views on it should be treated with caution. No specific personal or institutional connection is apparent from the provided profile for B056, B037, B007 or B012.
